s: Prometheus is subject to Prometheus’s punishment (until Zeus is overthrown)
q: Now, there is set no limit to my woe Till Zeus be hurled from his omnipotence.

s: Zeus is destined to suffer the future fall of Zeus (through his own counsels and a marriage)
q: Wooing a bride, his ruin he shall win.

s: Io is a daughter of Inachus
q: Daughter of Inachus; I know thee driven,

s: the future fall of Zeus is caused by Zeus’s child (the child overcomes his sire)
q: The child she bears him shall o’ercome his sire.

s: Hera hates her
q: she whom Hera’s hate Now harasses o’er leagues and leagues of land.

s: Argus is a herdsman (earth-born and malevolent)
q: but ever at my side, A herdsman by his heifer, Argus moved, Earth-born, malevolent of mood, and peered, With myriad eyes, where’er my feet would roam.

s: Argus has myriad eyes (for watching Io)
q: Argus moved, Earth-born, malevolent of mood, and peered, With myriad eyes, where’er my feet would roam.

s: Epaphus is a child of Io (dark and divinely conceived)
q: and thou shalt bear A child, dark Epaphus

s: Epaphus is named for Zeus’s touch (the touch that gives him life)
q: his very name Memorial of Zeus’ touch that gave him life.

s: Themis gives prophecy to Prometheus (as the ancient Titaness)
q: Such knowledge of the future Themis gave, The ancient Titaness, to me her son.

s: the gadfly is a scourge (of divine infliction)
q: Still maddened by the gadfly’s sting, the scourge Of God’s infliction, roam the weary world.

s: Caucasus is a world-topping peak (with a river descending from it)
q: till thou come Right to the very Caucasus, the peak That overtops the world, and from its brows The river pants in spray its wrathful stream.

s: Canopus is a town (at the verge of land and sea)
q: There lieth, at the verge of land and sea, Where Nilus issues thro’ the silted sand, A town, Canopus called

s: Io is loved by Zeus (with passionate desire)
q: Ay, thou art she whose beauty fired the breast Of Zeus with passion;

s: Nile flows through Canopus
q: Where Nilus issues thro’ the silted sand, A town, Canopus called

s: Io is harassed by Hera (because of Zeus’s passion)
q: she whom Hera’s hate Now harasses o’er leagues and leagues of land.

s: Io is stung by the gadfly (continually)
q: Still maddened by the gadfly’s sting, the scourge Of God’s infliction, roam the weary world.

s: Io is horned horned (as now ye see me)
q: And horned as now ye see me, poison-stung By the envenomed bitings of the brize,

s: Io undergoes Io’s wandering (through the world)
q: Still maddened by the gadfly’s sting, the scourge Of God’s infliction, roam the weary world.

s: Io is destined to bear Epaphus (at Canopus)
q: There lieth, at the verge of land and sea, Where Nilus issues thro’ the silted sand, A town, Canopus called: and there at length Shall Zeus renew the reason in thy brain With the mere touch and contact of his hand Fraught now with fear no more: and thou shalt bear A child, dark Epaphus

s: Io is destined to found new abode (in the land of the Nile)
q: There, Io, at the last, hath Fate ordained, For thee and for thy race, the charge to found, Far from thy native shore, a new abode.

s: Prometheus is a gods (immortal deity)
q: Why should I fear, who am immortal too?

s: Prometheus is buried by the storm and earthquake (in the shattered rocky ravine)
q: The rocks are rent with fire and earthquake, and fall, burying PROMETHEUS in the ruins.

s: Zeus has authority authority (in heaven; momentary)
q: Let him put forth his power, attest his sway, Howe’er he will—a momentary show, A little brief authority in heaven!

s: Zeus possesses Zeus's eagle (as an eagle-hound)
q: Back to the daylight shall thou come, and there The eagle-hound of Zeus, red-ravening, fell With greed, shall tatter piecemeal all thy flesh

s: Zeus is threatened by the future fall of Zeus (through a destined marriage)
q: Such wedlock as shall bring his doom on him, Flung from his kingship to oblivion’s lap!

s: the future fall of Zeus is caused by the threatened marriage of Zeus (according to Prometheus)
q: Such wedlock as shall bring his doom on him, Flung from his kingship to oblivion’s lap!

s: the threatened marriage of Zeus causes the future fall of Zeus (destined to bring about his overthrow)
q: Such wedlock as shall bring his doom on him, Flung from his kingship to oblivion’s lap!

s: Prometheus gives the stolen fire (to perishable men)
q: Trickster and sinner against gods, by giving The stolen fire to perishable men!

s: Hermes serves Zeus (as his herald)
q: Better, forsooth, be bond-slave to a crag, Than true-born herald unto Zeus the Sire!

s: Hermes demands information about the threatened marriage of Zeus (on Zeus's behalf)
q: the Sire supreme doth bid thee tell What is the wedlock which thou vauntest now, Whereby he falleth from supremacy?

s: Chorus supports Prometheus (compassionately and loyally)
q: Nay, at his side, whate’er befall, I will abide, endure it all!

s: Io suffers banishment (mateless)
q: A shudder to my soul is sent, Beholding Io’s doom forlorn— By Hera’s malice put to scorn, Roaming in mateless banishment

s: Hera persecutes Io (through malice)
q: By Hera’s malice put to scorn, Roaming in mateless banishment.

s: Prometheus has bonds these shaming bonds (shaming)
q: No mangling torture, no, nor sleight of power There is, by which he shall compel my speech, Until these shaming bonds be loosed from me.

s: Cronos is father of Zeus (as his father)
q: Ay, then the curse his father Cronos spake As he fell helpless from his agelong throne, Shall be fulfilled unto the utterance!

s: Cronos curses the future fall of Zeus (when falling from his throne)
q: Ay, then the curse his father Cronos spake As he fell helpless from his agelong throne, Shall be fulfilled unto the utterance!

s: Earth is mother of Prometheus (addressed by Prometheus)
q: O holy Earth, O mother mine! O Sky, that biddest speed along Thy vault the common Light divine,— Be witness of my wrong!

s: the Fates ordain Prometheus’s punishment (as an inescapable destiny)
q: Into the net the Fates ordain— The vast, illimitable pain!

s: Necessity is revered by gods
q: Yet do the wise revere Necessity.

s: Prometheus endures Prometheus’s punishment (without yielding to Zeus)
q: Ay—but mark this: mine heritage of pain I would not barter for thy servitude.

s: Prometheus hates gods (because they repay kindness with wrong)
q: Mark a plain word—I loathe all gods that are, Who reaped my kindness and repay with wrong.

s: Prometheus opposes Zeus (defiantly)
q: I reck of Zeus as something less than nought.

s: Prometheus knows how it may be foiled
q: No god but I can manifest to him A rescue from such ruin as impends— I know it, I, and how it may be foiled.

s: Prometheus refuses to reveal my speech (until these shaming bonds be loosed)
q: No mangling torture, no, nor sleight of power There is, by which he shall compel my speech, Until these shaming bonds be loosed from me.

s: Prometheus foresees the future fall of Zeus (as the fulfillment of Cronos's curse)
q: And yet shall Zeus, for all his stubborn pride, Be brought to low estate! aha, he schemes Such wedlock as shall bring his doom on him, Flung from his kingship to oblivion’s lap!

s: Aeschylus wrote nearly a hundred (during his life)
q: The surviving dramas of Aeschylus are seven in number, though he is believed to have written nearly a hundred during his life of sixty-nine years, from 525 B.C. to 456 B.C.

s: The Suppliant Maidens depicts the flight of the Danaids from Egypt to Argos (to escape forced marriage)
q: Its topic—the flight of the daughters of Danaus from Egypt to Argos, in order to escape from a forced bridal with their first-cousins, the sons of Aegyptus—is legendary

s: Danaus accompanies Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus (during their flight to Argos)
q: The maidens, accompanied by their father Danaes, have fled from Egypt and arrived at Argos

s: Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus are daughters of Danaus
q: the flight of the daughters of Danaus from Egypt to Argos

s: the forced bridal of the Danaids is with their first-cousins, the sons of Aegyptus
q: in order to escape from a forced bridal with their first-cousins, the sons of Aegyptus

s: Argos provides sanctuary to Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus (after their flight from Egypt)
q: The maidens, accompanied by their father Danaes, have fled from Egypt and arrived at Argos, to take sanctuary there

s: Aphrodite intervenes in the Danaids’ acquittal (in the probable final play of the trilogy)
q: The final play was probably called _The Danaides_, and described the acquittal of the brides through some intervention of Aphrodite

s: Pindar describes Chorus of the Daughters of Danaus (as honourably enthroned)
q: Pindar, Aeschylus’ contemporary, actually describes the once suppliant maidens as honourably enthroned

s: Aeschylus lived for sixty-nine years
q: The surviving dramas of Aeschylus are seven in number, though he is believed to have written nearly a hundred during his life of sixty-nine years, from 525 B.C. to 456 B.C.

s: Atossa is a Queen-mother of the Persian kingdom
q: Against the piteous want of manliness on the part of the returning Xerxes, we may well set the grave and dignified patriotism of Atossa, the Queen-mother of the Persian kingdom

s: Atossa is queen mother of the Persian kingdom
q: the grave and dignified patriotism of Atossa, the Queen-mother of the Persian kingdom

s: Darius is a royal phantom (evoked from the shadowland)
q: the royal phantom of Darius, evoked from the shadowland by the libations of Atossa and by the appealing cries of the Chorus

s: The Seven against Thebes is a third part of a trilogy (the House of Laius trilogy)
q: But the third part, as we have said, survives under the name given to it by Aristophanes, the _Seven against Thebes_

s: the House of Laius trilogy is also called The House of Laius (collectively)
q: It is the third part of a Trilogy which might have been called, collectively, _The House of Laius_.

s: The Seven against Thebes is set in the Cadmea (the Citadel of Cadmus)
q: The scene of action is the Cadmea, or Citadel of Cadmus

s: the Cadmea is the Citadel of Cadmus
q: The scene of action is the Cadmea, or Citadel of Cadmus

s: The Seven against Thebes depicts the Seven against Thebes war (as an attack on the Cadmea)
q: it opens with an exhortation by Eteocles to his Cadmeans that they should “quit them like men” against the onslaught of Polynices and his Argive allies

s: Aeschylus fought at the Battle of Marathon
q: That he fought at Marathon in 490, and at Salamis in 480 B.C. is a strongly accredited tradition

s: Eteocles is a son of Oedipus (one of the two princes)
q: The two sons quarrelled over the succession, then agreed on a compromise; then fell at variance again, and finally slew each other in single combat.

s: Polynices is a son of Oedipus (one of the two princes)
q: The two sons quarrelled over the succession, then agreed on a compromise; then fell at variance again, and finally slew each other in single combat.

s: Eteocles is killed by Polynices (in single combat)
q: The two sons quarrelled over the succession, then agreed on a compromise; then fell at variance again, and finally slew each other in single combat.

s: Polynices is killed by Eteocles (in single combat)
q: The two sons quarrelled over the succession, then agreed on a compromise; then fell at variance again, and finally slew each other in single combat.

s: Antigone is sister of Eteocles
q: It ends with the news of the death of the two princes, and the lamentations of their two sisters, Antigone and Ismene.

s: Antigone opposes the decree against Polynices’ burial (by defying the decree)
q: Against the latter sentence Antigone protests, and defies the decree

s: Thebes is not mentioned in The Seven against Thebes (despite the play’s traditional title)
q: Thebes is _never_ mentioned.

s: Oedipus is son of Laius (though raised by another king and queen)
q: Meantime his real father, Laius, on _his_ way to consult the god at Delphi, met his unknown son returning from that shrine

s: Oedipus marries Iokaste (without knowing she is his mother)
q: he wandered on, and found the now kingless Thebes in the grasp of the Sphinx monster, over whom he triumphed, and was rewarded by the hand of Iokaste, his own mother

s: Aeschylus fought at Persian defeat at Salamis
q: That he fought at Marathon in 490, and at Salamis in 480 B.C. is a strongly accredited tradition

s: Prometheus is condemned by Zeus (for his benevolence towards oppressed mankind)
q: For his benevolence towards oppressed mankind, Prometheus is condemned by Zeus to uncounted ages of pain and torment

s: Prometheus is punished by Zeus (for aiding humanity)
q: For his benevolence towards oppressed mankind, Prometheus is condemned by Zeus to uncounted ages of pain and torment

s: Zeus faces dethronement (in the lapse of ages)
q: So deadly is this secret, that Zeus will, in the lapse of ages, be forced to reconcile himself with Prometheus, to escape dethronement.

s: the sea nymphs remain with Prometheus (sharing his fate through the catastrophe)
q: they remain by Prometheus to the end, and share his fate, literally in the crack of doom.

s: the seven surviving dramas of Aeschylus has count seven
q: The surviving dramas of Aeschylus are seven in number

s: Aeschylean drama includes the Orestean Trilogy
q: This Trilogy is the masterpiece of the Aeschylean Drama

s: the Orestean Trilogy is composed of the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Eumenides
q: it survives, for us, in one instance only, viz. the Orestean Trilogy, comprising the _Agamemnon_, the _Libation-Bearers_, and the _Eumenides_, or _Furies_.

s: The Suppliant Maidens is a mythical drama
q: Its topic—the flight of the daughters of Danaus from Egypt to Argos, in order to escape from a forced bridal with their first-cousins, the sons of Aegyptus—is legendary, and the lyric element predominates in the play as a whole.
